title: Exploring sand and water
keyIdea: Dry sand pours and runs, like water does, so a dry sand castle falls down into a heap. Add a little water and the sand gets darker and sticks together, so it keeps the shape of the bucket and makes a castle. Water pours too, and it fills a cup until the cup is full: then no more fits, and the extra spills over. The words to use are wet, dry, pour, full and empty.

kid: Dry sand pours. It runs out of your hand. Tip a bucket of dry sand and it falls down in a heap.
Pour some water on the sand. Now it is wet. Wet sand is dark. It sticks together.
Fill a bucket with wet sand. Pat it down. Tip it over and lift it up. A castle! It keeps its shape.
Pour water in a cup. Stop at the top. Now it is full. Pour more and it spills.
adult: In England this sits in the EYFS area Understanding the World. Development Matters (2021) asks children from birth to three to explore materials with different properties and to explore natural materials, indoors and outside. Sand and water play also builds Mathematics (full, empty, capacity) and Communication and Language (wet, dry, pour). In the US, the Head Start Early Learning Outcomes Framework lists it under Scientific Reasoning: Exploration and Discovery.

Why it works: dry sand is lots of tiny hard grains that roll past each other, so it flows and settles into a low cone. A little water makes thin films between the grains. These water bridges pull the grains together, so damp sand holds a shape. Too much water fills the gaps, the pull is lost, and the sand turns runny again, which is why a castle on very wet sand slumps.

Common mistakes to watch for: toddlers often think any sand makes a castle, or that water will make sand fall apart; they keep pouring into a full cup because full is a new idea; and they call sand wet or dry by touch alone. Say the words as they play, let them feel both kinds, and ask which one kept its shape.

In the lab your child scoops dry sand into a bucket, tips it out and watches it fall into a heap, waters the sand and sees it get darker, tips out a wet sand castle that stands up, and pours water until 3 cups are full. Every step works with big buttons or by tapping the picture. Read the Challenge aloud together.

familyTip: At the sandpit or with a tray of sand at home, make one castle with dry sand and one with damp sand. Ask: which one stood up? Then give a cup and a jug and say stop when it is full.

visual.caption: Dry sand or wet sand? Drag each one, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: scoop dry sand and watch it pour, tip out a dry heap and a wet castle, water the sand and fill cups until they are full.

practice.prompt: Which sand makes a good castle?
practice.hint: Which sand sticks together when you pat it?
practice.explain: Wet sand sticks together, so it keeps the shape of the bucket.

practice.prompt: You scoop {n} scoops of sand into the bucket. How many scoops?
practice.hint: Count 1 for each scoop of sand.
practice.explain: {n} scoops went into the bucket. Count them one at a time.

practice.prompt: You make {a} castles. Then you make {b} more. How many castles?
practice.hint: Start at {a} and count on {b} more castles.

practice.prompt: The cup is full. You pour in more water. What happens?
practice.hint: Full means the water is right up to the top.
practice.explain: A full cup has no room left, so the extra water spills over.

pool.prompt: Which sand pours out of your hand?
pool.explain: Dry sand pours and runs. Wet sand sticks in lumps.

pool.prompt: You tip out a bucket of dry sand. What do you get?
pool.explain: Dry sand does not stick, so it falls down into a heap.

pool.prompt: What does a little water do to sand?
pool.hint: Think of the sand you use for a castle.
pool.explain: A little water makes sand stick together, so it keeps a shape.

pool.hint: Look at the sand where the water went.
pool.explain: Wet sand looks darker than dry sand.

pool.prompt: {n} cups are full. {k} cups are empty. How many cups in all?
pool.hint: Count the full cups, then count on the empty ones.
pool.explain: {n} full cups and {k} empty cups make {=n+k} cups.

pool.prompt: A cup has no water in it. What word do we use?
pool.hint: Is there anything inside the cup?
pool.explain: A cup with nothing in it is empty. A cup up to the top is full.

pool.prompt: You have {b} buckets of sand. You tip out {t}. How many are still full?
pool.hint: Start at {b} and take away the {t} you tipped out.

pool.prompt: Your castle will not stand up. What can you add?
pool.explain: A little water makes the sand stick, so the castle can stand up.
